855.title: Edmund Campion and Margaret Clitherow
855.hook: English Catholics executed for their faith under Elizabeth I
855.howItsDone: Catholics honor Edmund Campion and Margaret Clitherow among the canonized martyrs of England and Wales, and some old English houses still show visitors their hidden priest holes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter Canisius and his little books of questions and answers. Your line was simple words. Today, a time when saying it at all could cost your life.

A knock at the door of a house in York. Somewhere inside there's a hidden place where a priest can disappear, and a place to keep the things needed for Mass. The woman of the house runs a butcher's shop with her husband. Her name is Margaret Clitherow. In the England of Elizabeth the First, sheltering a Catholic priest is a crime that can be punished by death. Earlier, a scholar from Oxford named Edmund Campion rode from house to house in disguise, saying Mass in homes like hers.
screen: `A KNOCK IN YORK.` → `A HIDDEN PLACE.` → `A SCHOLAR IN DISGUISE.`

segments.voice: Edmund Campion was a brilliant Oxford man, admired at court. He became Catholic, joined the Jesuits abroad, and came back to England secretly, knowing what it might cost. He preached in private houses and moved on before he could be caught. In a letter to the queen's council, he wrote that the cost had been counted and the work begun, and could not be stopped. He was arrested, tortured, tried for treason, and executed. At his trial he argued that in condemning him, they condemned their own ancestors, whose faith he shared. Catholic families built hiding places into their houses, so priests could vanish when searchers came. They're known as priest holes. Margaret Clitherow, the butcher's wife, hid priests in York. When she was arrested, she refused to enter a plea, so there would be no trial at which her children and household could be made to testify. For refusing, the law of the time had her crushed to death. Then, the honest frame. In that century, Christians of different churches put one another to death, in England and elsewhere. Protestants died under Catholic rulers too. The Church honors its martyrs, and in our own time has also asked forgiveness for violence done in its name. The Gospel that Campion and Clitherow held to says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

segments.voice: Bring to mind people somewhere in the world today who are in danger for what they believe, or for what they don't, any faith, any place, and simply hold them: the ones hiding, the ones in prison, the families waiting for news. If you pray, pray for them, and for those who persecute them, as Jesus asked. If you don't, simply wish them safety and freedom.
Priest holes. Hiding places built into Catholic homes, so a priest could vanish when searchers came, like the one in Margaret Clitherow's house in York.
Your line: hidden priests. Faith kept alive in hidden rooms. Day eight hundred fifty-five, done.

856.title: Galileo, honestly (1633)
856.hook: the Church condemned Galileo; in 1992 John Paul II acknowledged the error
856.howItsDone: The Vatican keeps an observatory and a Pontifical Academy of Sciences, and Catholic teaching holds that faith and reason cannot truly contradict each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Edmund Campion, Margaret Clitherow, and the hidden places in their houses, the priest holes. Your line was hidden priests. Today, a story the Church tells against itself.

A tube of glass and wood, pointed at the night sky over Italy. Through it, the moon has mountains. Jupiter has small lights circling it. The man at the eyepiece writes it all up in a short book with a Latin title, the Starry Messenger. He is a Catholic, a professor, and very sure of himself. What he's seeing points to an idea that the earth moves around the sun, and some in the Church will call that idea against the Scriptures. His name is Galileo.
screen: `MOUNTAINS ON THE MOON.` → `THE STARRY MESSENGER.` → `THE EARTH MOVES.`

segments.voice: First, the argument. Galileo's critics pointed to passages like the one where Joshua commands the sun to stand still. If the sun stands still, they said, it must normally move. Galileo answered in a long letter, quoting a churchman of his day: the Holy Spirit means to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how the heavens go. Scripture, he argued, speaks the way ordinary people speak about sunrise. Second, the condemnation. The Holy Office in Rome ruled against the idea, and later put Galileo on trial. He was made to kneel and formally renounce the view that the earth moves. He spent the rest of his life confined to his house near Florence, and kept working. He was not burned, and he remained a Catholic. Third, the legend. People say that as he rose from his knees he muttered, and yet it moves. It's a good line, but it isn't in the trial records; it's a story told later. Fourth, the admission. Centuries later, Pope John Paul the Second asked for the case to be studied again. Speaking to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, he acknowledged that the theologians who condemned Galileo had erred, and called the affair a tragic mutual misunderstanding. A pope had said, in public, that the condemnation was a mistake. Some Catholics pair this with the Psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God." For those who pray it, the Psalm and the telescope look at the same sky.

857.title: Matteo Ricci in China (1552–1610)
857.hook: a Jesuit who learned Chinese, dressed as a scholar and made friends
857.howItsDone: Catholic missionaries and bishops speak of inculturation when they bring the liturgy, music and art of a local culture into the life of the Church, and Ricci is often remembered in that conversation, especially by Jesuits.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Galileo: a condemnation, and much later a pope admitting in public that it was an error. Your line was the error, admitted.

An Italian with a long beard sits in a scholar's silk robe, in a city at the far end of the world from Rome. His guests haven't come for a sermon. They've come for his maps, his clocks, his mathematics, and his memory, which could do tricks they had never seen. They argue with him about Confucius. He argues back, in their language, quoting their classics. Some become his friends. A few become Christians. His name is Matteo Ricci, a Jesuit, and the long word for what he was trying to do is today's word.
screen: `A SCHOLAR'S SILK ROBE.` → `MAPS, CLOCKS, MEMORY.` → `ARGUING IN THEIR LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Inculturation means letting the faith take root in a culture, speaking its language and wearing its clothes, without stopping being itself. Ricci never used the word; it came much later. But his life is one of the stories Catholics reach for to explain it. First, the language. Ricci and his companions studied Chinese for years, spoken and written, until he could write books Chinese scholars read seriously. Second, the clothes. At first the Jesuits dressed like Buddhist monks. Then Ricci noticed who was listening: the educated class who read Confucius. So he changed into a scholar's robes. Third, friendship. One of his early books in Chinese was a small collection of sayings on friendship, drawn from Western writers. In effect it said: I came a long way, to be your friend. One friend, the scholar Xu Guangqi, became a Christian and worked with him translating geometry. Fourth, the hard question. Ricci judged that Chinese Christians could keep honoring Confucius and the ancestors as a civil and family custom, not worship. Others in the Church strongly disagreed. The argument went on long after his death, and Church rulings on it changed over time. So inculturation isn't a slogan. It's a question you keep asking: what belongs to the faith, and what is simply the coat it arrived in? Paul put the instinct in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "I became all things to all men, that I might save all."

858.title: Rose of Lima (1586–1617)
858.hook: a young woman in a garden hut in Lima, remembered as the first canonized saint of the Americas
858.howItsDone: Catholics in Peru and across Latin America keep the feast of Saint Rose of Lima, often with processions, and some Dominican laypeople look to her as a model of holiness lived outside a convent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Matteo Ricci in a scholar's robe, and inculturation: the faith taking root in a culture. Your line was friendship first.

At the back of a family garden in Lima, in Peru, stands a hut with barely room for one person. Inside, a young woman sews. Her needlework and the flowers she grows help keep her family fed. Some days the door opens onto a different job: sick and hungry people from the city, whom she brings into a room of her parents' house and nurses herself. She never enters a convent. She never travels. Yet the Church remembers her as the first person from the Americas to be named a saint. Her baptismal name was Isabel. In time she was called Rose.
screen: `A HUT IN A GARDEN.` → `NEEDLEWORK AND FLOWERS.` → `THE SICK IN HER PARENTS' HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the name came from a servant who saw her as a baby and thought her face looked like a rose. She kept it. First, a life at home. Rose wanted a life given to God, but she didn't join an enclosed convent. She became a Dominican tertiary: a laywoman who follows the spirituality of the Dominicans while living in the world. Her cloister was a hut in the family garden. Second, the work of her hands. She sewed and sold flowers to help her family, and took the poor and sick into her parents' house to nurse them herself. Third, the hard part, told honestly. Rose practiced severe penances: fasting, sleeping on hard boards, wearing things meant to hurt. Her biographers called these heroic. Some Catholics today read them more carefully, as signs of a fierce love that shouldn't be copied, and the Church doesn't ask anyone to imitate them. Fourth, the cross at the center. Her spirituality kept returning to the suffering Christ. Paul put it in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." She belonged to a city of new wealth and old wounds, of conquerors and the conquered. When the Church named her a saint, the Americas had their first. Lima still keeps her feast as its own.

859.title: Martin de Porres (1579–1639)
859.hook: a mixed-race Dominican brother in Lima, with a broom, a clinic, and mice he fed
859.howItsDone: Catholics often show Saint Martin de Porres with a broom, and some parishes and schools named for him run food pantries or outreach to the poor; he is invoked by people who face racial prejudice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rose of Lima, a Dominican tertiary nursing the sick in her parents' house. Your line was first of the americas. Today, the same city.

Statues of him often show the same things: a Dominican in a black and white habit, a dark-skinned face, and in his hand, not a book or a sword, but a broom. Sometimes a dog, a cat and a mouse eat from one bowl at his feet. It looks like a children's picture. It's actually a summary of a life. He swept floors, cut hair, set bones, fed the hungry at the door, and for a long time held the lowest place in his house. Today, Martin de Porres.
screen: `NOT A BOOK, NOT A SWORD.` → `A BROOM.` → `A DOG, A CAT, A MOUSE.`

segments.voice: First, where he started. Martin was born in Lima, the son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed Black woman. His father didn't acknowledge him at first. The colonial world sorted people by race, and Martin landed near the bottom. Second, a door half open. He trained as a barber, which then also meant small surgery and setting bones. Then he asked to join the Dominicans. The rules of the time kept men like him from full vows, so he entered as a donado, a lay helper who gave his work to the house. He swept. He cleaned. Only later did the community admit him as a professed brother. Third, the clinic. As infirmarian he cared for sick friars, and the care spread out the door: to slaves, to the city's poor, to anyone who came. Fourth, the stories. Tradition says that when the priory was short of money, Martin offered to be sold to pay its debts. Tradition says he struck a deal with the house mice: stay in the garden, and I'll feed you there. Some are legends, retold many times; even so, they point one way. He took the lowest place and made it holy. Jesus describes himself in that place, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am in the midst of you, as he that serveth." The broom isn't decoration. It's the claim his life makes: sweeping a floor for God is not a lesser kind of prayer.
screen: `A NOBLEMAN'S SON, NOT ACKNOWLEDGED.` · `A DONADO: THE LOWEST PLACE.` · `THE CLINIC OUT THE DOOR.` · `SELL ME. FEED THE MICE.` · then, large: `AS HE THAT SERVETH.`

860.title: Peter Claver (1580–1654)
860.hook: in Cartagena he met every slave ship and called himself the slave of the slaves
860.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Peter Claver and invoke him as a patron of enslaved people and of ministry to African-descended communities; some parishes mark it with prayer for victims of human trafficking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martin de Porres, the donado of Lima who swept floors and nursed the city's poor. Your line was the saint with a broom. Today, the Caribbean.

Word comes into the port of Cartagena that a ship has been sighted. For the merchants, that means cargo. For the people in the hold, it means the end of a voyage they were forced to make in chains, sick, starving, some of them dying. And for one Spanish Jesuit, it means going down to the docks with baskets of food, water, lemons and medicine, and climbing down into the hold. This is a hard story, and it should be told plainly. Today, Peter Claver.
screen: `A SHIP IS SIGHTED.` → `PEOPLE IN CHAINS IN THE HOLD.` → `A PRIEST CLIMBS DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Cartagena, on the Caribbean coast of what is now Colombia, was a port where enslaved Africans were brought and sold. Claver was sent there as a young man. Before he left Spain, an elderly Jesuit brother, Alphonsus Rodriguez, a doorkeeper, had urged him toward the people no one cared for. Second, the docks. When a ship came in, Claver went below decks. He brought food and water first, and washed and bandaged the sick. He used interpreters to speak to people in their own languages, and taught and baptized those who asked. He followed them into the yards where they were held, and later to plantations and hospitals. Third, the vow. At his final vows as a Jesuit, he signed his name with a Latin phrase: the slave of the Africans forever. It passed down as slave of the slaves. Fourth, the honest part. Claver didn't end the slave trade, and the Church of his day did not condemn it outright. He served inside an evil he could not stop, and those who tell his story now try to remember both: his love, and the system it ran into. Jesus's words in Matthew read like his job description, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink." Near the end Claver was sick and largely forgotten, poorly cared for himself. The Church later named him a saint, and Catholics invoke him as a patron of enslaved people.
screen: `CARTAGENA: A SLAVE PORT.` · `DOWN INTO THE HOLD.` · `SLAVE OF THE AFRICANS FOREVER.` · `HE COULDN'T STOP IT. HE SERVED.` · then, large: `I WAS HUNGRY, AND YOU GAVE ME TO EAT.`

segments.voice: Forced labor didn't end with the ships: people are still trafficked, held in debt, made to work without pay or freedom, sometimes close to where you live. Let them be present, without names, the way the people in the hold were present to Claver. If you pray, ask Peter Claver to pray for them, or pray an Our Father slowly; if not, simply stay with them, and let it cost you a little.
Peter Claver. A Spanish Jesuit in Cartagena who met the slave ships with food and medicine, and called himself the slave of the Africans forever.

861.title: Kateri Tekakwitha (1656–1680)
861.hook: a Mohawk and Algonquin woman, scarred by smallpox, later named a saint
861.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Kateri Tekakwitha, and her shrines in New York and Quebec draw pilgrims; Indigenous Catholic gatherings in North America often bear her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter Claver, climbing into the holds of slave ships with food and water. Your line was slave of the slaves.

A girl in a Mohawk village keeps a blanket pulled over her head when she goes outside. Smallpox swept through when she was small. It took her parents, marked her face and weakened her eyes, so bright light hurts. Her mother had been an Algonquin Christian; her father was Mohawk. She grows up in her uncle's longhouse, quiet, skilled with her hands, and saying no to the marriage her family wants for her. Then black-robed priests come to the village. Today, Kateri Tekakwitha.
screen: `A BLANKET OVER HER HEAD.` → `SMALLPOX TOOK HER PARENTS.` → `SHE SAYS NO TO MARRIAGE.`

segments.voice: First, two peoples in one person. Kateri carried both, Mohawk and Algonquin. Catholics remember her as a saint of Indigenous North America, and some Indigenous Catholics speak of her as one of their own, not as someone the missionaries made. Second, baptism. She asked a Jesuit, Jacques de Lamberville, to teach her, and he baptized her. She took the name Catherine; Kateri is the Mohawk way of saying it. Some in her village turned on her. The early accounts tell of mockery and threats, some of it because she refused to work on Sundays. Third, the journey. She left, on foot and by canoe, for a Christian mission village near Montreal, where Mohawk and other Native Christians lived together. There she prayed long hours, cared for the sick and old, and promised God never to marry. Her penances were severe, and she was never strong. She died young. Fourth, the lily. The Jesuits who knew her wrote her life, and one recorded that after she died, the scars on her face faded. Catholics hand it down as his testimony, an eyewitness's word. The Church named her Venerable, then Blessed, then a saint. People call her the Lily of the Mohawks, and some Catholics hear in that name a line from the Song of Songs, in the Douay-Rheims: "As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters." A lily, growing where no one expected it.
screen: `MOHAWK AND ALGONQUIN.` · `BAPTIZED: KATERI, FOR CATHERINE.` · `TO THE MISSION BY CANOE.` · `THE SCARS FADED, THEY WROTE.` · then, large: `AS THE LILY AMONG THORNS.`

segments.voice: Across the Americas, Native communities keep the faith in their own languages, songs and memories, some of them painful; let one come to mind, a nation whose land you live on or a name you've heard. If you pray, ask Kateri Tekakwitha to pray for them; if not, hold them with respect. And if this week's stories have been heavy, let yourself rest here.
Kateri Tekakwitha. A Mohawk and Algonquin woman, scarred by smallpox, baptized against her village's wishes, who walked to a mission and gave her life to prayer and the sick.
